items.title: 2.10.3 Method to Find Global Extrema of a Continuous Functions Defined on a Closed Interval [a, b]

source_refs.note: Book p. 54: 2.10.3 three-step method for global extrema on [a, b], Example 20 (derivative misprinted as x^4 - 4x)

items: Find all critical points of the function within the interval \([a, b]\).
Find values of the function at critical points and at end points of the interval.
The largest of these values is the global maximum value, and the smallest is the global minimum value.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why only these points? On a closed interval a continuous function has a global maximum and a global minimum (2.10.2). If such an extreme value occurs inside the interval it occurs at a critical point (the graph turns there); otherwise it occurs at an end point. So the candidates are: critical points inside \([a, b]\) and the two end points \(a\) and \(b\).
We do not need to decide whether each candidate is a maximum or a minimum: we simply compare the values.

blocks.title: Example 20
blocks.problem: Find the global extreme values of \(f(x) = x^{4} - 4x\) on \([-2, 3]\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{4} - 4x\) ...(1), on the closed interval \([-2, 3]\).
To find: the global maximum and global minimum values.
Method: the three-step method above: \(f\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous on \([-2, 3]\) and its global extrema are among the values at the critical points and at the end points.

Step 1: Differentiate equation (1)
The book prints \(f'(x) = x^{4} - 4x\) ...(2) (see the Book correction below). Differentiating correctly:
\[f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 4 \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: power rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{4}) = 4x^{3}\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}(4x) = 4\). The book's next line, \(4x^{3} - 4 = 0\), uses the correct derivative.

Step 2: Critical points
From equation (2) it is clear that \(f'(x)\) exists on \([-2, 3]\). For stationary points we solve \(f'(x) = 0\):
\[4x^{3} - 4 = 0\]
\[4(x^{3} - 1) = 0\]
\[(x - 1)(x^{2} + x + 1) = 0\]
Why: difference of cubes, \(x^{3} - 1 = (x - 1)(x^{2} + x + 1)\).

Step 3: Real roots only
Either \(x - 1 = 0\) or \(x^{2} + x + 1 = 0\). The equation \(x^{2} + x + 1 = 0\) has complex roots (its discriminant is \(1 - 4 = -3 < 0\)), so the only real stationary point is \(x = 1\), and it lies in \([-2, 3]\).
Why: only real points of the interval can be critical points.

Step 4: Values at the critical point and the end points
\[f(1) = 1^{4} - 4(1) = -3\]
\[f(-2) = (-2)^{4} - 4(-2) = 16 + 8 = 24\]
\[f(3) = 3^{4} - 4(3) = 81 - 12 = 69\]
Why: step 2 of the method: the end points must be included.

Step 5: Compare
From the values \(-3\), \(24\), \(69\): the largest is 69 and the smallest is \(-3\).
Why: step 3 of the method.

Check: \(f'(x) < 0\) for \(x < 1\) and \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(x > 1\) (for example \(f'(0) = -4\), \(f'(2) = 28\)), so \(f\) falls from 24 to \(-3\) and then rises to 69. The lowest point is at \(x = 1\) and the highest at the right end \(x = 3\).
blocks.answer: The global maximum is \(f(3) = 69\) and the global minimum is \(f(1) = -3\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 20 prints the derivative as \(f'(x) = x^{4} - 4x\) ...(2), which repeats \(f(x)\). The correct derivative is \(f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 4\). The next line (\(4x^{3} - 4 = 0\)) and the final answer use the correct derivative.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Lay out the candidates in one line: "Critical point value: \(f(1) = -3\); end point values: \(f(-2) = 24\), \(f(3) = 69\)". Then state the global maximum and minimum with the points where they occur.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Candidates for global extrema on \([a, b]\): critical points inside \([a, b]\) and the end points \(a\), \(b\).
2. Evaluate \(f\) at every candidate; largest = global maximum value, smallest = global minimum value.
3. Ignore critical points outside \([a, b]\) and complex roots.
4. Example 20: global maximum \(f(3) = 69\), global minimum \(f(1) = -3\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the end points: in Example 20 the global maximum is at the end point \(x = 3\).
2. Putting the critical point into \(f'\) instead of \(f\) when finding the values.
3. Keeping a critical point that lies outside the interval.
